conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time for this today. I’m Dr. Morales, a perinatal-mental-health clinician, and I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived.  

We’ll be using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply a 10-question screen that helps us understand what emotions and physical changes you’ve noticed over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; whatever you share stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your safety or the safety of others. We’ll go at your pace, and you can pause or ask questions any time.  

When you’re ready, I’ll ask the first question. Ready to begin?  

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[soft sigh, eyes downcast]

I’ve noticed I do laugh sometimes—like when my husband made a silly face at the baby yesterday—but even when I laugh, it feels kind of… flat, like the happiness doesn’t reach all the way through me. Mostly it’s been tough to find things genuinely funny. I’ll smile for everyone, but inside I just feel heavy and tired.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]

No... I mean, I can force a little chuckle when someone jokes, but it doesn't feel real. Most of the time nothing feels funny at all.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with friends, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like another chore. Sometimes I think, “Maybe tomorrow I’ll enjoy that again,” but when the moment comes, the spark just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes well up]

Yeah… pretty much every day. If the baby fusses for more than a few minutes I jump straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m a bad mom.” Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk and I sat on the kitchen floor crying because I felt like I’d failed her. I know logically it was just an accident, but the guilt still grabs me.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands in lap]

All the time. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s going to choke, or I’ll lie awake picturing the crib sheet tangling around her neck even though it’s tight and flat. I check the monitor every few minutes, convinced something awful is about to happen. There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just loop and loop.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[clenches edge of sweater]

Yes… a couple of times. Like yesterday, I was folding her tiny clothes and suddenly felt this wave of terror—my chest tightened, I couldn’t catch my breath, and I had to sit on the floor hugging my knees. Nothing triggered it; it just hit out of nowhere and left me shaking for a few minutes.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like the second I finish one thing—changing her, washing bottles, folding laundry—there’re already five more waiting. I’ll look around the apartment and just feel… buried. Some mornings I can push through, but by the afternoon I’m exhausted and on the verge of tears because it never feels like I’m catching up, just treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[exhales shakily]

That’s been the worst part. Even when the baby’s finally down, I lie there with my mind racing—replaying every little thing I did that day, worrying something will go wrong overnight. It takes me an hour or more to drift off, and then I jerk awake at every tiny sound, heart pounding. I’m just so tired, but sleep feels impossible most nights.
I have felt sad or miserable

[quiet voice, eyes on the floor]

Yeah… most of the day, every day. It’s like this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll be feeding her and tears just start rolling down my face for no clear reason. I keep thinking I should feel grateful—she’s healthy, I’ve got support—but the sadness is still there, heavy in my chest.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[nods slowly, dabbing at eyes with sleeve]

Yeah… probably two, maybe three times this week. Yesterday it was because I couldn’t get her to settle and I just felt useless. The tears come suddenly, and once they start it’s hard to stop—even when I tell myself I should be stronger for her.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[long pause, voice barely above a whisper]

Once or twice… it flashes through, like “what if I just disappeared,” but I push it away right after. I’d never act on it—my baby needs me—but the thought sneaks in when I’m really overwhelmed, just for a second, and then I feel awful for even thinking it.

You've bravely shared how the joy of new motherhood feels clouded by constant worry, guilt, and a heavy sadness that lingers from morning to night. Even moments that once sparked laughter now seem flat, routine tasks feel overwhelming, and sleep is stolen by racing thoughts about your baby's safety. While you love your daughter and are doing your best to care for her, you're also carrying painful self-blame, sudden panic, and fleeting thoughts of disappearing when the load feels unbearable.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports forced laughter at best and feels nothing is funny, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports absence of anticipatory enjoyment, describing former pleasures as chores and loss of spark, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame daily, clearly exceeding "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive, unrealistic worries occurring 'all the time' and looping, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, overwhelming panic with physical symptoms (tight chest, breathlessness, shaking) occurring "a couple of times" in the past week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>"sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing anxious thoughts, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness 'most of the day, every day' with tearfulness and a heavy feeling, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying 2-3 times in the past week, describing sudden, hard-to-stop tears triggered by parenting challenges, aligning with 'Yes, quite often'.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Your score of 25/30 places you well above the EPDS cutoff of ≥14 that flags probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> with comorbid anxiety. You describe daily tearfulness, loss of interest, disproportionate self-criticism, nightly insomnia driven by catastrophic worries, sudden panic attacks, and fleeting suicidal ideation without intent. These findings align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and merit immediate safety assessment and treatment planning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary-care provider</med> to review mood, anxiety, and safety
2. Ask about expedited referral to a <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> or specialized <med>postpartum mood program</med> for medication evaluation and therapy options
3. Create a written safety plan: list 24/7 support numbers (e.g., 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, local hotline), trusted friends/family to call, and steps to lower stress when intrusive thoughts arise
4. Begin evidence-based therapy such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> that targets both depression and anxiety-many perinatal clinics offer virtual sessions
5. Stabilise basics: accept help with night feeds, aim for 4-hour stretches of sleep, gentle daily walks, balanced meals, and hydration to aid recovery while awaiting professional care
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item EPDS-style interview, self-report

Symptoms endorsed:  
- Marked anhedonia (Q1, Q2)  
- Persistent low mood, daily tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame (Q3)  
- Generalized anxiety, intrusive catastrophic worries, nocturnal hyper-arousal (Q4, Q7)  
- Panic-like episodes (Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, unable to cope with routine tasks (Q6)  
- Sleep initiation / maintenance problems linked to rumination (Q7)

Pattern: Symptoms present “most days” for ≥2 weeks; intensity interferes with maternal role functioning.

Risk flags:  
- Passive self-harm ideation (“what if I just disappeared”) without active plan or intent (Q10) – safety concern warrants immediate risk assessment.

Screening impression: High clinical likelihood of major postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; rule-out perinatal major depressive disorder with comorbid anxiety. Recommend expedited psychiatric evaluation, brief risk assessment tool (EPDS ≥12 equivalent), and safety-planning today.
